claims.text: Sublingual NTG is the most effective drug for an acute attack,
claims.quote: To relieve symptoms during an acute attack, sublingual nitroglycerin is the most effective medication (2, 3).

claims.text: and can also be taken to prevent angina before exertion.
claims.quote: Sublingual nitroglycerin is given for an acute attack or for prevention before exertion.

claims.text: Long-acting doses: ISDN 10–20 mg PO TID, up to 40 mg TID;
claims.quote: 10–20 mg orally 3 times a day; can be increased to 40 mg 3 times a day
claims.locator: table: Medications for Coronary Artery Disease (Isosorbide dinitrate)

claims.text: ISMN SR 30 or 60 mg once daily, up to 120 mg;
claims.quote: 30 or 60 mg orally once a day, increased to 120 mg or, rarely, 240 mg
claims.locator: table: Medications for Coronary Artery Disease (Isosorbide mononitrate, sustained-release)

claims.text: NTG patch 0.2–0.8 mg/hour applied 6–9 AM and removed 12–14 hours later.
claims.quote: 0.2–0.8 mg/hour applied between 6:00 and 9:00 AM and removed 12–14 hours later to avoid tolerance
claims.locator: table: Medications for Coronary Artery Disease (Nitroglycerin patches)

claims.text: Also contraindicated with sGC stimulators such as riociguat (hypotension).
claims.quote: Do not use NITROSTAT in patients who are taking the soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators, such as riociguat. Concomitant use can cause hypotension.

claims.text: Contraindicated in severe anemia (methemoglobin can worsen it).
claims.quote: NITROSTAT is contraindicated in patients with severe anemia (large doses of nitroglycerin may cause oxidation of hemoglobin to methemoglobin and could exacerbate anemia).
Nitrate therapy may aggravate the angina caused by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

claims.text: Severe hypotension can occur even with small doses, especially with aortic or mitral stenosis, constrictive pericarditis, volume depletion or existing hypotension.
claims.quote: Severe hypotension, particularly with upright posture, may occur with small doses of nitroglycerin particularly in patients with constrictive pericarditis, aortic or mitral stenosis, patients who may be volume-depleted, or are already hypotensive.

claims.text: Overdose: severe hypotension, throbbing headache, methemoglobinemia with cyanosis, syncope.
claims.quote: Nitrate overdosage may result in: severe hypotension, persistent throbbing headache, vertigo, palpitation, visual disturbance, flushing and perspiring skin (later becoming cold and cyanotic), nausea and vomiting (possibly with colic and even bloody diarrhea), syncope (especially in the upright posture), methemoglobinemia with cyanosis and anorexia,

claims.text: No specific antagonist: raise central fluid volume (shock position, IV saline);
claims.quote: No specific antagonist to the vasodilator effects of nitroglycerin is known. Keep the patient recumbent in a shock position and comfortably warm. Passive movement of the extremities may aid venous return. Intravenous infusion of normal saline or similar fluid may also be necessary.

claims.text: methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV for methemoglobinemia unless G6PD deficiency;
claims.quote: If methemoglobinemia is present, administration of methylene blue (1% solution), 1-2 mg per kilogram of body weight intravenously, may be required unless the patient is known to have G-6-PD deficiency.
As epinephrine is ineffective in reversing the severe hypotensive events associated with overdosage, it is not recommended for resuscitation.
